extractions.name: Example: Finding the General Solution When the Characteristic Equation Has Imaginary Roots
extractions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} + 25y =0.
$$
extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y=e^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x}  = \lambda e^{\lambda x}, \qquad \frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2}  = \lambda^2 e^{\lambda x} .
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+25{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+25) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding characteristic equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-25 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 5\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y = P\cos{5x} + Q\sin{5x}.
$$

extractions.problem: Suppose that a matrix $A$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=\lambda (\lambda +1)^{3}(\lambda -2)^{4},$ the rank of $(A-2I)^{2}$ equals $7,$ and the rank of $(A-2I)^{3}$ equals $6.$ If a basis of ${\mathbb{R}}^{8}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $A$, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2?$

extractions.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda =2,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ is a vector $\mathbf{v}$ such that 

$$
(A-2I)^{3}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}\,\text{and}\,(A-2I)^{2}\mathbf{v}\ne \mathbf{0}.
$$

Notice that $A$ must be an $8\times 8$ matrix.

- Since the rank of $(A-2I)^{2}$ equals $7,$ then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-2I)^{2}=8-7=1.
$$

So, the solutions to $(A-2I)^{2}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{2}$ of dimension $1$ in ${\mathbb{R}}^{8}.$

- Since the rank of $(A-2I)^{3}$ equals $6,$  then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-2I)^{3}=8-6=2.
$$

So, the solutions to $(A-2I)^{3}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{3}$ of dimension $2$ in ${\mathbb{R}}^{8}.$

Since $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{2}$ is a subspace of dimension $1$ in $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{3}$, which is a subspace of dimension $2,$ our basis can contain only $1$ vector that lies in $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{3}$ but does not lie in $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{2}.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(A-2I)^{3}-\text{nullity}(A-2I)^{2}=2-1=1
$$

 generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2.$

extractions.problem:
Consider the linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ with matrix representation $T,$ given by

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

A tetrahedron $M$ has vertices at $(0,-6,0),(6,0,0),$ $(-2,1,0),$ and $(0,-1,2).$ Which of the following are coordinates of the vertices of ${M}^{′}$, the image of $M$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}?$

I. $(0,2,-8)$

II. $(-2,2,1)$

III. $(6,-1,0)$

extractions.worked_solution:
To find the image of $M$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$, we first create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of $M:$

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 & -2 & 0 \\ -6 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under $\mathbf{T}$ by calculating the matrix product $TX:$

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 6 & -2 & 0 \\ -6 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 & -2 & 0 \\ 12 & -12 & 2 & 2 \\ -6 & 0 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the respective vertices of ${M}^{′}$ are $(0,12,-6),(6,-12,0),(-2,2,1),(0,2,-3).$ 

So, the correct answer is "II only."

extractions.problem:
Consider the linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ with matrix representation $T,$ given by

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

A tetrahedron $Y$ has vertices at $(-4,-2,0),(5,2,0),$ $(2,-1,0),$ and $(5,-2,2).$ Which of the following are coordinates of the vertices of ${Y}^{′}$, the image of $Y$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}?$

I. $(-4,1,0)$

II. $(5,-1,7)$

III. $(-2,7,0)$

extractions.worked_solution:
To find the image of $Y$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$, we first create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of $Y:$

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 5 & 2 & 5 \\ -2 & 2 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under $\mathbf{T}$ by calculating the matrix product $TX:$

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 & 5 & 2 & 5 \\ -2 & 2 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -5 & -2 & -3 \\ -10 & 13 & 7 & 17 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the respective vertices of ${Y}^{′}$ are $(4,-10,0),(-5,13,0),(-2,7,0),(-3,17,-6).$ 

So, the correct answer is "III only."

extractions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $(2a+1)({a}^{2}+a+10)?$

extractions.worked_solution:
We distribute both terms of the binomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2a+1)({a}^{2}+a+10) & = \\ 2a({a}^{2}+a+10)+1({a}^{2}+a+10) & = \\ 2{a}^{3}+2{a}^{2}+20a+{a}^{2}+a+10 & = \\ 2{a}^{3}+3{a}^{2}+21a+10\end{aligned}
$$

extractions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $(q+1)({q}^{2}+7q+2)?$

extractions.worked_solution:
We distribute both terms of the binomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}(q+1)({q}^{2}+7q+2) & = \\ q({q}^{2}+7q+2)+1({q}^{2}+7q+2) & = \\ {q}^{3}+7{q}^{2}+2q+{q}^{2}+7q+2 & = \\ {q}^{3}+8{q}^{2}+9q+2\end{aligned}
$$

extractions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $(q+1)({q}^{2}+7q+2)?$

extractions.worked_solution:
We distribute both terms of the binomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}(q+1)({q}^{2}+7q+2) & = \\ q({q}^{2}+7q+2)+1({q}^{2}+7q+2) & = \\ {q}^{3}+7{q}^{2}+2q+{q}^{2}+7q+2 & = \\ {q}^{3}+8{q}^{2}+9q+2\end{aligned}
$$

Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+16{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+16) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+16=0.
$$

 

The auxiliary equation has pure imaginary roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-16 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 4\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y=P\operatorname{cos} 4x+Q\operatorname{sin} 4x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+16{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+16) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+16=0.
$$

 

The auxiliary equation has pure imaginary roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-16 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 4\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y=P\operatorname{cos} 4x+Q\operatorname{sin} 4x.\end{aligned}
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+11{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+11) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+11=0.
$$

 

The auxiliary equation has pure imaginary roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+11 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-11 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \sqrt{11}\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y=P\operatorname{cos} (\sqrt{11}x)+Q\operatorname{sin} (\sqrt{11}x).\end{aligned}
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+3{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+3=0.
$$

 

The auxiliary equation has pure imaginary roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+3 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-3 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \sqrt{3}\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y=P\operatorname{cos} (\sqrt{3}x)+Q\operatorname{sin} (\sqrt{3}x).\end{aligned}
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+49{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+49) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+49=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation has pure imaginary roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+49 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-49 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 7\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y=P\operatorname{cos} 7x+Q\operatorname{sin} 7x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now let's find the constants $P$ and $Q.$ 

Substituting $y(0)=-2$ into the general solution gives

$$
P=-2.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=7.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$

$$
{y}^{′}=-7P\operatorname{sin} 7x+7Q\operatorname{cos} 7x
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=7$ into the above gives

$$
7Q=7.
$$

So we have $P=-2$ and $Q=1.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=-2\operatorname{cos} 7x+\operatorname{sin} 7x.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+100{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+100) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+100=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation has pure imaginary roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+100 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-100 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 10\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y=P\operatorname{cos} 10x+Q\operatorname{sin} 10x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now let's find the constants $P$ and $Q.$ 

Substituting $y(0)=5$ into the general solution gives

$$
P=5.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=20.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$

$$
{y}^{′}=-10P\operatorname{sin} 10x+10Q\operatorname{cos} 10x
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=20$ into the above gives

$$
10Q=20.
$$

So we have $P=5$ and $Q=2.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=5\operatorname{cos} 10x+2\operatorname{sin} 10x.
$$

extractions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2y=0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+2{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+2=0.
$$

 

The auxiliary equation has pure imaginary roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-2 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \sqrt{2}\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y=P\operatorname{cos} (\sqrt{2}x)+Q\operatorname{sin} (\sqrt{2}x).\end{aligned}
$$

Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+81{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+81) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+81=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation has pure imaginary roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+81 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-81 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 9\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y=P\operatorname{cos} (9x)+Q\operatorname{sin} (9x).\end{aligned}
$$

extractions.name: Example: Identifying Non-Solutions of a Second-Order Homogeneous ODEs
extractions.problem:
Given that $y = y(t)$ satisfies the equation $y'' - 4y' + 85y = 0,$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?

I. $-2e^{2t}\cos{9t} + 7e^{2t}\sin{9t}$

II. $e^{2t}\cos{9t}+3e^{2t}\sin{3t}$

III. $-6e^{2t}\sin{9t}$
extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y = e^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
y' = \lambda e^{\lambda t}, \qquad y'' = \lambda^2 e^{\lambda t} .
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}-4\lambda {e}^{\lambda t}+85{e}^{\lambda t} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda t}({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +85) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding characteristic equation is

$$
\lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 85 = 0,
$$

and we can solve it by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +85 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4)-4+85 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2}+81 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-81 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm 9\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm 9\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\lambda = 2 \pm 9 \textrm{i}$ are the complex roots of the characteristic equation, the general solution takes the form

$$
y = e^{2t} \left( P \cos 9t + Q \sin 9t \right).
$$

Finally, we need to determine whether each of the given functions takes the form shown above.

- Function I takes the above form with $P=-2$ and $Q=7.$ So, it is a solution to the given ODE.

- Function II does *not* take the above form. It contains $\sin 3t,$ which is not included in the above form. So, it is *not* a solution to the given ODE.

- Function III takes the above form with $P=0$ and $Q=-6.$ So, it is a solution to the given ODE.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

extractions.problem: Given that $y=y(x)$ satisfies the equation ${y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+50y=0,$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+2\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+50{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +50) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +50=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +50 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +1)-1+50 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2}+49 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2} & =-49 \\ \lambda +1 & =\pm 7\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-1\pm 7\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =-1\pm 7\text{i}$ are the complex roots of the auxiliary equation.

Thus, any linear combination of the functions $\text{Re}({e}^{(-1+7\text{i})x})={e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos} 7x$ and $\text{Im}({e}^{(-1+7\text{i})x})={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin} 7x$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $50{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin} 7x$ is not a solution.

extractions.problem: Given that $y=y(x)$ satisfies the equation ${y}^{″}+y=0,$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+1=0.
$$

 

Solving the auxiliary equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\lambda =\pm \text{i}$ are the purely imaginary roots of the auxiliary equation. 

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions $\text{Re}({e}^{\text{i}x})=\operatorname{cos} x$ and $\text{Im}({e}^{\text{i}x})=\operatorname{sin} x$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $\operatorname{sin} 2x$ is not a solution.

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+8\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+17{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +17) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +17=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +17 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +16)-16+17 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)^{2}+1 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda +4 & =\pm \text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-4\pm \text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =-4\pm \text{i}$ are the complex roots of the auxiliary equation.

Thus, any linear combination of the functions $\text{Re}({e}^{(-4+\text{i})x})={e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos} x$ and $\text{Im}({e}^{(-4+\text{i})x})={e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin} x$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only ${e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos} x-4{e}^{x}$ is not a solution.

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda t}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda t},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}+64{e}^{\lambda t} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda t}({\lambda }^{2}+64) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+64=0.
$$

Solving the auxiliary equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+64 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-64 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 8\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\lambda =\pm 8\text{i}$ are the (purely imaginary) roots of the auxiliary equation. 

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions $\text{Re}({e}^{8\text{i}t})=\operatorname{cos} 8t$ and $\text{Im}({e}^{8\text{i}t})=\operatorname{sin} 8t$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $\operatorname{sin} 8t-2\operatorname{cos} 4t$ is not a solution.

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+4\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+20{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +20) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +20=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +20 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4)-4+20 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2}+16 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =-16 \\ \lambda +2 & =\pm 4\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-2\pm 4\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =-2\pm 4\text{i}$ are the complex roots of the auxiliary equation.

Thus, any linear combination of the functions $\text{Re}({e}^{(-2+4\text{i})x})={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos} 4x$ and $\text{Im}({e}^{(-2+4\text{i})x})={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin} 4x$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $4{e}^{-2x}+{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin} 4x$ is not a solution.

extractions.problem: Given that $y=y(x)$ satisfies the equation ${y}^{″}-12{y}^{′}+40y=0,$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?

$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +40=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +40 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +36)-36+40 & =0 \\ (\lambda -6)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -6)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda -6 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =6\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =6\pm 2\text{i}$ are the complex roots of the auxiliary equation.

Among the given options, only $3{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos} 2x+\operatorname{sin} 2x$ is not a solution.

extractions.problem: Given that $y=y(x)$ satisfies the equation ${y}^{″}+100y=0,$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+100{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+100) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+100=0.
$$

Solving the auxiliary equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+100 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-100 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 10\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\lambda =\pm 10\text{i}$ are the (purely imaginary) roots of the auxiliary equation. 

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions $\text{Re}({e}^{10\text{i}x})=\operatorname{cos} 10x$ and $\text{Im}({e}^{10\text{i}x})=\operatorname{sin} 10x$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $\frac{\operatorname{cos} 5x}{10}$ is not a solution.

extractions.name: Example: Finding the Complex Solutions of a Characteristic Equation
extractions.problem: Consider the equation $y'' + 10y' + 34y  = 0,$ where $y = y(t).$ If $y = e^{\lambda t}$ is a solution, then what is $\lambda?$
extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y = e^{\lambda t}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
y' = \lambda e^{\lambda t}, \qquad y'' = \lambda^2 e^{\lambda t} .
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}+10\lambda {e}^{\lambda t}+34{e}^{\lambda t} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda t}({\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +34) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding characteristic equation is

$$
\lambda^2 + 10\lambda + 34  = 0,
$$

and we can solve it by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +34 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +25)-25+34 & =0 \\ (\lambda +5)^{2}+9 & =0 \\ (\lambda +5)^{2} & =-9 \\ \lambda +5 & =\pm 3\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-5\pm 3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  $\lambda = - 5 \pm 3\textrm{i}$ are the complex roots of the auxiliary equation.

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+12\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+40{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+12\lambda +40) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+12\lambda +40=0
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+12\lambda +40 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+12\lambda +36)-36+40 & =0 \\ (\lambda +6)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda +6)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda +6 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-6\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  $\lambda =-6\pm 2\text{i}$ are the complex roots of the auxiliary equation.

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+4\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+8{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +8) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +8=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +8 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4)-4+8 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda +2 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-2\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  $\lambda =-2\pm 2\text{i}$ are the complex roots of the auxiliary equation.

Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda t}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda t},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}+3{e}^{\lambda t} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda t}({\lambda }^{2}+3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+3=0.
$$

Solving the auxiliary equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+3 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-3 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \sqrt{3}\,\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{3}\,\text{i}$ are the (purely imaginary) roots of the auxiliary equation.

extractions.problem: Consider the equation ${y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}+6y=0,$ where $y=y(x).$ If $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ is a solution, then $\lambda =$

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-4\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+6{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +6) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +6=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +6 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4)-4+6 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2}+2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-2 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm \sqrt{2}\,\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm \sqrt{2}\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  $\lambda =2\pm \sqrt{2}\,\text{i}$ are the complex roots of the auxiliary equation.

extractions.problem: Consider the equation ${y}^{″}+49y=0,$ where $y=y(x).$ If $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ is a solution, then $\lambda =$

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+49{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+49) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+49=0.
$$

Solving the auxiliary equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+49 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-49 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 7\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  $\lambda =\pm 7\text{i}$ are the (purely imaginary) roots of the auxiliary equation.

extractions.problem: Consider the equation ${y}^{″}+y=0,$ where $y=y(t).$ If $y={e}^{\lambda t}$ is a solution, then $\lambda =$

extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda t}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda t},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}+{e}^{\lambda t} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda t}({\lambda }^{2}+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+1=0.
$$

Solving the auxiliary equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  $\lambda =\pm \text{i}$ are the (purely imaginary) roots of the auxiliary equation.

extractions.name: Example: Finding the General Solution When the Characteristic Equation Has Complex Roots
extractions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} - 4 \frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} + 20y =0.
$$
extractions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y=e^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x}  = \lambda e^{\lambda x}, \qquad \frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2}  = \lambda^2 e^{\lambda x} .
$$

Substituting the above into our ODE gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-4\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+20{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +20) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding characteristic equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +20 & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can solve it by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +20 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4)-4+20 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2}+16 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-16 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm 4\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos} 4x+Q\operatorname{sin} 4x).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(3{w}^{2}+w+5)({w}^{2}+w+1) & = \\ 3{w}^{2}({w}^{2}+w+1)+w({w}^{2}+w+1)+5({w}^{2}+w+1) & = \\ 3{w}^{4}+3{w}^{3}+3{w}^{2}+{w}^{3}+{w}^{2}+w+5{w}^{2}+5w+5 & = \\ 3{w}^{4}+4{w}^{3}+9{w}^{2}+6w+5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=4,$ $b=9,$ and $c=6.$ So, 

$$
a+b+c=4+9+6=19.
$$

We distribute all three terms of the trinomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}({s}^{2}+2s-1)({s}^{2}-s+2) & = \\ {s}^{2}({s}^{2}-s+2)+2s({s}^{2}-s+2)-1({s}^{2}-s+2) & = \\ {s}^{4}-{s}^{3}+2{s}^{2}+2{s}^{3}-2{s}^{2}+4s-{s}^{2}+s-2 & = \\ {s}^{4}+{s}^{3}-{s}^{2}+5s-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=1,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=5.$ So, 

$$
a+b+c=1+(-1)+5=5.
$$

We distribute all three terms of the trinomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}({t}^{2}-6t+9)({t}^{2}-4t+4) & = \\ {t}^{2}({t}^{2}-4t+4)+(-6t)({t}^{2}-4t+4)+9({t}^{2}-4t+4) & = \\ {t}^{4}-4{t}^{3}+4{t}^{2}-6{t}^{3}+24{t}^{2}-24t+9{t}^{2}-36t+36 & = \\ {t}^{4}-10{t}^{3}+37{t}^{2}-60t+36\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=-10,$ $b=37,$ and $c=-60.$ So, 

$$
a+b+c=-10+37+(-60)=-33.
$$

We distribute all three terms of the trinomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}({p}^{2}+p+1)({p}^{2}+3p+1) & = \\ {p}^{2}({p}^{2}+3p+1)+p({p}^{2}+3p+1)+1({p}^{2}+3p+1) & = \\ {p}^{4}+3{p}^{3}+{p}^{2}+{p}^{3}+3{p}^{2}+p+{p}^{2}+3p+1 & = \\ {p}^{4}+4{p}^{3}+5{p}^{2}+4p+1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=4,$ $b=5,$ and $c=4.$ So, 

$$
a+b+c=4+5+4=13.
$$

We distribute all three terms of the trinomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}({t}^{2}+t+2)({t}^{2}+2t+1) & = \\ {t}^{2}({t}^{2}+2t+1)+t({t}^{2}+2t+1)+2({t}^{2}+2t+1) & = \\ {t}^{4}+2{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}+{t}^{3}+2{t}^{2}+t+2{t}^{2}+4t+2 & = \\ {t}^{4}+3{t}^{3}+5{t}^{2}+5t+2 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=3,$ $b=5,$ and $c=5.$ So, 

$$
a+b+c=3+5+5=13.
$$

We distribute all three terms of the trinomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}^{2}+3y+2)({y}^{2}+7y+1) & = \\ {y}^{2}({y}^{2}+7y+1)+3y({y}^{2}+7y+1)+2({y}^{2}+7y+1) & = \\ {y}^{4}+7{y}^{3}+{y}^{2}+3{y}^{3}+21{y}^{2}+3y+2{y}^{2}+14y+2 & = \\ {y}^{4}+10{y}^{3}+24{y}^{2}+17y+2 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=10,$ $b=24,$ and $c=17.$ So, 

$$
a+b+c=10+24+17=51.
$$

We distribute all three terms of the trinomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}({s}^{2}+2s-1)({s}^{2}-s+2) & = \\ {s}^{2}({s}^{2}-s+2)+2s({s}^{2}-s+2)-1({s}^{2}-s+2) & = \\ {s}^{4}-{s}^{3}+2{s}^{2}+2{s}^{3}-2{s}^{2}+4s-{s}^{2}+s-2 & = \\ {s}^{4}+{s}^{3}-{s}^{2}+5s-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=1,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=5.$ So, 

$$
a+b+c=1+(-1)+5=5.
$$

We distribute all three terms of the trinomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2{d}^{2}-d-2)({d}^{2}-2d+2) & = \\ 2{d}^{2}({d}^{2}-2d+2)-d({d}^{2}-2d+2)-2({d}^{2}-2d+2) & = \\ 2{d}^{4}-4{d}^{3}+4{d}^{2}-{d}^{3}+2{d}^{2}-2d-2{d}^{2}+4d-4 & = \\ 2{d}^{4}-5{d}^{3}+4{d}^{2}+2d-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=-5,$ $b=4,$ and $c=2.$ So, 

$$
a+b+c=-5+4+2=1.
$$

extractions.problem: A function $f(x)=4x-\frac{6}{x}$ is defined on an interval $[a,6]$, where $a$ is a negative parameter. Calculate $a$ such that the average rate of  change over $[a,6]$ is equal to $3.$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let's calculate the average rate of change of $f(x)$ over the interval $[a,6]$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{Δ}f}{\mathrm{Δ}x} & =\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} \\  & =\frac{(4(6)-\frac{6}{6})-(4(a)-\frac{6}{a})}{6-a} \\  & =\frac{23-4a+\frac{6}{a}}{6-a} \\  & =\frac{23-4a+\frac{6}{a}}{6-a}\cdot \frac{a}{a} \\  & =\frac{23a-4{a}^{2}+6}{a(6-a)} \\  & =\frac{6+23a-4{a}^{2}}{a(6-a)} \\  & =\frac{(6-a)(1+4a)}{a(6-a)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(6-a)}(1+4a)}{a\cancel{(6-a)}} \\  & =\frac{1+4a}{a}\end{aligned}
$$

We want $\frac{\mathrm{Δ}f}{\mathrm{Δ}x}$ be equal to $3$, so 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1+4a}{a} & =3 \\ 1+4a & =3a \\ a & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $a<0$, we conclude that $a=-1$ and the interval is $[-1,6].$

extractions.problem: Solve the congruence $14x≡6\,(\text{mod}\,55).$

extractions.worked_solution:
Recall that a linear congruence $ax≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)$ has a unique solution modulo $n$ if and only if $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1.$  

In the given congruence, we have $a=14$ and $n=55$, where

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(14,55)=1.
$$

So, our congruence does indeed have a unique solution.

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $14\,(\text{mod}\,55).$ To find the inverse of $14\,(\text{mod}\,55)$, use the extended Euclidean algorithm.

First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{array}{ccccc}{\color{red}55} & = & {\color{red}14\cdot 3} & + & {\color{red}13} \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ {\color{blue}14} & = & {\color{blue}13\cdot 1} & + & {\color{blue}1}\end{array}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\color{red}13} & ={\color{red}55-14\cdot 3} \\ {\color{blue}1} & ={\color{blue}14-13}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we back-substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\color{blue}1} & ={\color{blue}14}-{\color{red}13} \\  & ={\color{blue}14}-{\color{red}(55-14\cdot 3)} \\  & =14\cdot 4-55\end{aligned}
$$

We can write this result in modulo $55,$ as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}14\cdot 4-55 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,55) \\ 14\cdot 4 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,55)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $14\cdot 4≡1\,(\text{mod}\,55),$ which means that $4$ is the multiplicative inverse of $14$ (modulo $55$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our original congruence by $4,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}14x & ≡6 &  & (\text{mod}\,55) \\ 4\cdot 14x & ≡4\cdot 6 &  & (\text{mod}\,55) \\ (4\cdot 14)x & ≡24 &  & (\text{mod}\,55) \\ 1\cdot x & ≡24 &  & (\text{mod}\,55) \\ x & ≡24 &  & (\text{mod}\,55)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x≡24\,(\text{mod}\,55).$

Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+2\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+26{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +26) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +26=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +26 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +1)-1+26 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2}+25 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2} & =-25 \\ \lambda +1 & =\pm 5\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-1\pm 5\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{-x}(P\operatorname{cos} 5x+Q\operatorname{sin} 5x).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
extractions.worked_solution:

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+8\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+18{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +18) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +18=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +18 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +16)-16+18 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)^{2}+2 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)^{2} & =-2 \\ \lambda +4 & =\pm \sqrt{2}\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-4\pm \sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{-4x}(P\operatorname{cos} \sqrt{2}x+Q\operatorname{sin} \sqrt{2}x).\end{aligned}
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+6\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+109{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +109) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +109=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +109 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +9)-9+109 & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)^{2}+100 & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)^{2} & =-100 \\ \lambda +3 & =\pm 10\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-3\pm 10\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{-3x}(P\operatorname{cos} 10x+Q\operatorname{sin} 10x).\end{aligned}
$$

extractions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-6\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+13y=0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-6\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+13{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +13) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +13=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +13 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9)-9+13 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda -3 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =3\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{3x}(P\operatorname{cos} 2x+Q\operatorname{sin} 2x).\end{aligned}
$$

extractions.problem: What is the coefficient of $v{w}^{2}$ in the product $(v+w)({v}^{2}+4vw+{w}^{2})?$

extractions.worked_solution:
We distribute both terms of the binomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}(v+w)({v}^{2}+4vw+{w}^{2}) & = \\ v({v}^{2}+4vw+{w}^{2})+w({v}^{2}+4vw+{w}^{2}) & = \\ {v}^{3}+4{v}^{2}w+v{w}^{2}+{v}^{2}w+4v{w}^{2}+{w}^{3} & = \\ {v}^{3}+5{v}^{2}w+5v{w}^{2}+{w}^{3} & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coefficient of $v{w}^{2}$ is $5.$

extractions.problem: Solve the congruence $17x≡9\,(\text{mod}\,50).$

extractions.worked_solution:
Recall that a linear congruence $ax≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)$ has a unique solution modulo $n$ if and only if $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1.$ 

In the given congruence, we have $a=17$ and $n=50$, where

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(17,50)=1.
$$

So, our congruence does indeed have a unique solution.

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $17\,(\text{mod}\,50).$ To find the inverse of $17\,(\text{mod}\,50)$, use the extended Euclidean algorithm.

First, we apply the forward reduction:  

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{array}{ccccc}{\color{red}50} & = & {\color{red}17\cdot 2} & + & {\color{red}16} \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ {\color{blue}17} & = & {\color{blue}16\cdot 1} & + & {\color{blue}1}\end{array}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\color{red}16} & ={\color{red}50-17\cdot 2} \\ {\color{blue}1} & ={\color{blue}17-16}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we back-substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\color{blue}1} & ={\color{blue}17}-{\color{red}16} \\  & ={\color{blue}17}-{\color{red}(50-17\cdot 2)} \\  & =17\cdot 3-50\end{aligned}
$$

We can write this result in modulo $50,$ as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}17\cdot 3-50 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,50) \\ 17\cdot 3 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,50)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $17\cdot 3≡1\,(\text{mod}\,50),$ which means that $3$ is the multiplicative inverse of $17$ (modulo $50$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our original congruence by $3,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}17x & ≡9 &  & (\text{mod}\,50) \\ 3\cdot 17x & ≡3\cdot 9 &  & (\text{mod}\,50) \\ (3\cdot 17)x & ≡27 &  & (\text{mod}\,50) \\ 1\cdot x & ≡27 &  & (\text{mod}\,50) \\ x & ≡27 &  & (\text{mod}\,50)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x≡27\,(\text{mod}\,50).$

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+8y=0.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-4\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+8{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +8) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +8=0.
$$

\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +8 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4)-4+8 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}

extractions.name: Question 11
extractions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+8y=0.
$$
extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-4\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+8{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +8) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +8=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +8 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4)-4+8 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos} 2x+Q\operatorname{sin} 2x).\end{aligned}
$$

extractions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3y=0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+2\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+3{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +3=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +3 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +1)-1+3 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2}+2 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2} & =-2 \\ \lambda +1 & =\pm \sqrt{2}\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-1\pm \sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{-x}(P\operatorname{cos} \sqrt{2}x+Q\operatorname{sin} \sqrt{2}x).\end{aligned}
$$

extractions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+20y=0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+4\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+20{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +20) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +20=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +20 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4)-4+20 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2}+16 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =-16 \\ \lambda +2 & =\pm 4\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-2\pm 4\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{-2x}(P\operatorname{cos} 4x+Q\operatorname{sin} 4x).\end{aligned}
$$
